title: Dressed Chicken Luwombo
author: Ssalongo Ssali
desc: Two whole chickens grilled golden over embers strewn with banana peels, stuffed with curried potatoes, trussed, wrapped in banana leaf with a third of the sauce each, and steamed three to four hours.
longDesc: This is luwombo built like a banquet dish rather than a household one, from the Daily Monitor's long-running food columnist. Three details make it: banana peels spread over the barely glowing embers, so the chickens take up banana smoke before they ever see a leaf; the chickens grilled whole and then stuffed with potatoes cooked in their own separate tomato sauce; and a steaming time of three to four hours for village chickens, or under an hour for broilers. It is a real distinction and worth respecting.
ingredients: Kayi — string, for trussing and tying
// Used in the method but absent from the printed list
equipment: Matooke stems, or a perforated metal colander
steps: // The grill
Get a charcoal stove or grill alight and fiercely hot, then let the embers die down until they are barely glowing.
Spread some banana peels over the embers.
Grill the chickens whole until they are a good golden brown. Remove and set aside.
// The sauce
Drop the tomatoes into boiling water for a few minutes, remove, peel off the skins and mash them coarsely with your fingers.
Heat cooking oil and fry the chopped shallots until translucent.
Add the garlic — holding back 2 teaspoons — and fry a few minutes.
Add two-thirds of the tomatoes, the grilled chickens and the tomato paste.
Simmer over low heat. Add salt, pepper, the butter, the bay leaf and some chicken stock.
// The stuffing
Peel and quarter the Irish potatoes.
In a second pan, heat oil and fry the chopped onions until translucent, then add the reserved garlic and fry a few minutes.
Add the remaining tomatoes, half the tomato paste, salt and pepper.
Add the potatoes, bring to the boil, and simmer covered about 10 minutes.
// Assembly
Stuff the two chickens with the potatoes and truss them with string.
Lay a luwombo leaf in a shallow bowl and set a chicken in it with the drumsticks facing up.
Spoon about a third of the sauce into the leaf.
Fold the ends of the banana leaf together and tie carefully with string, without piercing the leaf.
// Steaming
Line a large saucepan with matooke stems, or use a perforated metal colander.
Set the luwombos inside, tuck banana leaves over the top and tie with string or banana fibre.
Steam over low heat until the chicken is tender — allow at least 3 to 4 hours for village chickens, or under an hour for broilers.
Serve the parcels closed.
chefTips: Banana peels on the embers. That is the detail to steal from this recipe — the chickens pick up banana smoke before they are ever wrapped, and it is why this tastes different from a luwombo that was only steamed.
Embers barely glowing, not fiery. Get the fire hot and then wait.
Three to four hours for a village chicken, under an hour for a broiler. That is the columnist's own distinction and it matters more than any other timing in the recipe.
Tie the leaf without piercing it. A punctured parcel leaks its sauce into the steaming water and you lose the point of the dish.
Reserve two teaspoons of garlic for the potato pan. The recipe splits the garlic between the two sauces and the printed list does not say so.
Cooking oil is used twice in the method and does not appear in the ingredient list at all. You need it; the amount is your judgement.
The same columnist published this recipe again the following year specifying margarine where this version says butter. Same writer, same dish, different fat, unreconciled — use either.
Matooke stems line the pan in place of banana leaf spines. A metal colander does the same job and the recipe says so.
commonMistakes: Grilling over flames instead of dying embers.
Steaming a village chicken for an hour.
Piercing the parcel when tying it.
Using all the garlic in the first sauce.
sources: Adapted from A. Kadumukasa Kironde II, 'Food that has typified Uganda since independence', Daily Monitor, 9 October 2022, and his 'Recipes that befit a king', Daily Monitor, 30 July 2023 — the banana peels over barely glowing embers, the whole-chicken grilling, the two-pan sauce and stuffing, the reserve-2-teaspoons-of-garlic instruction, the 4 tablespoons of tomato paste, the third-of-the-sauce-per-leaf measure, the matooke-stem lining and the 3-to-4-hours-or-under-an-hour-for-broilers steaming are all his.
The 2022 column lists butter; the 2023 column lists margarine. Same author, same recipe, not reconciled. Both are recorded.

Cooking oil appears in the method of both columns and in neither ingredient list. The 2022 column lists garlic with no quantity while its method specifies reserving 2 teaspoons; the 2023 column has no consolidated ingredient list at all and names its ingredients inside the method.
Kironde was the Daily Monitor's food columnist over many years and has since died.
storage: Refrigerate in the parcels up to 3 days.
reheating: Steam the parcels again for 15 minutes.
healthBenefits: Chicken supplies complete protein, niacin, selenium and vitamin B6.
Steamed in leaf rather than fried, so no additional fat after the sauce.
Tomatoes, onions and potatoes all go into the same dish.
Contains dairy in the butter or margarine.
culturalNote: Luwombo was created in 1887 for Kabaka Mwanga II by his chef Kawuta, and this version is closer to that court register than a household one: two whole birds, a stuffing, a separate sauce, and half a day of steaming. Its author wrote it for the sixtieth anniversary of independence, recalling a Kampala where restaurants were scarce and the local woteli establishments in the peri-urban areas served Ugandan food.
